function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
**Triangulation metrics** are the quantitative indicators you use to judge how “good” a triangulation is—whether it’s a mesh of triangles for a terrain model, a finite‑element grid, a Delaunay triangulation of points, or any other set of connected triangles. They let you compare different triangulations, tune algorithms, and verify that the output satisfies the quality requirements of your application. Below is a quick‑look at the most common categories and the specific metrics that fall under each one. | Category | Typical Metrics | What they tell you | |----------|-----------------|--------------------| | **Geometric quality** | • **Minimum angle** – smallest interior angle in any triangle.
• **Maximum angle** – largest interior angle.
• **Aspect ratio** – ratio of longest side to shortest altitude (or circumradius to inradius).
• **Edge‑length ratio** – ratio of longest to shortest edge in a triangle.
• **Triangle area distribution** – histogram of triangle areas.
• **Skewness / shape factor** – how far a triangle deviates from an equilateral shape. | Detects “skinny” or poorly shaped triangles that can degrade numerical stability or visual quality. | | **Topological consistency** | • **Number of triangles** – total count.
• **Number of vertices** – total count.
• **Connectivity checks** – e.g., no dangling edges, no duplicate triangles. | Ensures the mesh is fully connected and free of topological errors. | | **Performance / resource usage** | • **Runtime** – wall‑clock time to generate the triangulation.
• **Memory footprint** – peak RAM used.
• **CPU cycles** – processor time consumed. | Helps benchmark algorithms and tune for speed or memory constraints. | | **Application‑specific** | • **Surface error** – difference between the triangulated surface and a reference (e.g., DEM error).
• **Coverage** – percentage of the domain that is actually triangulated.
• **Feature preservation** – how well sharp edges or ridges are maintained. | Measures how well the triangulation serves its end‑use (e.g., GIS, CFD, graphics). | ### How a “triangulation metrics” function typically works 1. **Input** – A triangulation data structure (list of vertices + list of triangle indices) or a file containing it. 2. **Processing** – * Iterate over each triangle. * Compute side lengths, angles, area, aspect ratio, etc. * Accumulate statistics (min/max/mean, histograms). * Optionally run performance timers or memory profilers. 3. **Output** – A structured report (often JSON or a Python dict) that contains: ```json { "num_triangles": 12345, "num_vertices": 6789, "min_angle_deg": 12.3, "max_angle_deg": 170.1, "aspect_ratio_mean": 1.45, "aspect_ratio_max": 3.67, "area_histogram": [ ... ], "runtime_sec": 0.42, "memory_mb": 12.7 } ``` 4. **Interpretation** – * A **minimum angle** below ~10° usually signals a problem. * An **aspect ratio** above ~3–4 indicates skinny triangles. * A **runtime** that grows super‑linearly with the number of points may hint at algorithmic inefficiency. ### Why you’d use them | Use case | Why metrics matter | |----------|--------------------| | **Mesh generation** | Guarantees that the mesh will not produce numerical instabilities in simulations. | | **Terrain modeling** | Ensures that the DEM accurately captures elevation changes without introducing artifacts. | | **Computer graphics** | Prevents visual glitches caused by poorly shaped polygons. | | **Algorithm comparison** | Lets you objectively decide between Delaunay, constrained Delaunay, or other triangulation methods. | | **Quality assurance** | Provides a repeatable, automated way to catch regressions when code changes. | --- #### Quick sanity check If you run a triangulation on a set of random points and get: * `min_angle_deg` ≈ 0.5° * `aspect_ratio_max` ≈ 10 …you probably have a lot of degenerate triangles that will wreak havoc in downstream processing. On the other hand, if `min_angle_deg` ≈ 30° and `aspect_ratio_max` ≈ 1.5, you’re in good shape. --- **Bottom line:** Triangulation metrics give you a numeric snapshot of the *shape*, *size*, *connectivity*, and *performance* of a triangulation. They’re the standard way to say “this mesh is fine” or “this mesh needs improvement.” If you’re building or evaluating a triangulation pipeline, you’ll almost always want to compute and log these metrics.
